Author: @paolosama
Content:
All true, but you don't mention the reasons behind the truths you cited. The so-called Italian Southern Question is not actually just an Italian issue but rather a problem that characterizes the entire Global South. In fact, all countries in sub-tropical and tropical regions have consistently experienced a certain level of backwardness over the past 2000 years.
The reason behind this phenomenon Is that the peoples of the Global South have experienced time as cyclical rather than linear since the dawn of time. The populations that migrated north in ancient times had to face the threat of winters: this is when days stopped repeating themselves identically because, in the north, seasons exist. Those who did not store food to withstand harsh winters perished, and over centuries, individuals with an inherent sense of linear time – consisting of a past, present, and future – were naturally selected.

This implies a sense of sacrifice in the present to secure well-being in the future (when winter arrives), a concept that first underpinned Christian morality (the past is sin, the present is sacrifice, the future is bliss in paradise) and later the scientific method (the past is ignorance, the present is research, the future is knowledge). Linear time allows societies to organize, develop, and ensures that every action is weighed based on its future consequences.

The issue facing the Global South arises from their cyclical perception of time, which prevents them from acting with the future in mind. This is because the ancestors of these populations did not need to do so to survive, as in tropical regions, food resources remain constant throughout the year, and each day repeats itself. This also explains why they are among the most easily corruptible peoples on the planet: better an egg today than a hen tomorrow if I cannot conceive of tomorrow.

Even the MOST florishing sub-tropical civilization, the Egyptian civilization, did not percieved time as linear. In fact, they believed that at the dawn of each morning, Ra would rise on his celestial chariot (the sun) and create the world anew with his light. This world would then be destroyed at the end of his journey across the sky at dusk, only to be recreated identically the following day, continuing in this way for eternity.

In conclusion, the Italian Southern Question has much deeper roots and is, above all, not solely an Italian issue but one that affects all tropical and subtropical regions of the world. If something is not necessary, natural selection eliminates it – this has been the case for the need to sacrifice in order to achieve something in the future, a concept perceived to a lesser extent by the peoples of the South.

Southern Italy, in fact, is genetically more similar to Greece and Turkey, at least at the time of Italy's unification, while the peoples of Northern Italy have French and Austrian ancestry.

Author: @sittingonatoilet2000
Content:
As an archaeologist who has delved deep into history, I believe the North-South divide in Italy can be traced back to the 13th century. Prior to this period, there was no clear socioeconomic division between the North and South. In fact, in earlier times, the southern part of the peninsula was significantly more developed than the north, as evidenced by the wealth of cities like Pompeii.

The division began with the rise of Italian city-states, which were concentrated in central and northern Italy. These city-states fostered a less hierarchical society, laying the groundwork for the Renaissance and capitalism (think of banks and maritime republics). In contrast, the South remained trapped in an extremely conservative absolute monarchy (the Spanish one), which, despite enjoying a rather wealthy state, ensured the miserable social conditions of its subjects, preventing and suppressing the emergence of a modern bourgeoisie. This explains why southern Italians, suffocated by the monarchy, found their only outlet for entrepreneurial expression in the "mafia," which was, in fact, a form of rebellion against the state.

Unfortunately, this situation persisted until 1861, when the Savoy monarchy, hailing from the far north, came to power and did little to favor the more remote regions of the kingdom. It wasn't until the early 20th century, under Fascist rule, that the South began to modernize, with the construction of basic state infrastructure. This explains the nostalgia for Mussolini among many older southerners, not to mention the results of the 1946 referendum, where the South was more inclined to support the monarchy.

The North, as mentioned, had a very different history from the late Middle Ages onwards: communes, the Renaissance, signories, maritime republics, and countless wars, with significant involvement from European states. These states, primarily France and Austria-Hungary, imparted a modernist imprint on the small duchies and kingdoms of central and northern Italy (while also plundering everything they could), especially Lombardy.

In my humble opinion, southern Italy's backwardness is due to a long history of oppressive monarchy, even at a time when the rest of Europe was moving towards modernity. While the situation is very different today, it will take a long time to change such a deeply rooted culture.

Regarding the issue of environmental disasters, I agree to a certain extent. However, if we were to apply the same logic, Japan would be the most depressed country in the world, which is clearly not the case.




Sono un archeologo e ho studiato molta storia nel corso della mia vita. A mio parere la frattura tra Nord e Sud Italia è tracciabile fin dal XIII secolo; nel periodo precedete non c'era una chiara divisione socioeconomica tra Nord e Sud, e piuttosto, nei periodi più remoti, abbiamo un centrosud ben più sviluppato rispetto al settentrione, basti pensare alla ricchezza di città come Pompei. La divisione inizia col periodo dei Comuni d'Italia, i quali si concentrarono notevolmente nel Centro e nel Nord Italia, dando vita ad una società meno verticalizzata, che diede seguito agli albori del Rinascimento e del Capitalismo (basti pensare alle banche e alle repubbliche marinare). Al contrario il Sud rimase cristallizzato in una monarchia assoluta MOLTO conservatrice (quella Spagnola), che pur beandosi di uno stato piuttosto ricco, rese miserabile la condizione sociale dei suoi sudditi, evitando e sopprimendo la nascita della borghesia moderna. Questo spiegherebbe come gli italiani del Sud, asfissiati dalla monarchia, trovarono unico sfogo di espressione imprenditoriale quello della "mafia", che, di fatto è una rivalsa sullo Stato. Questo, ahimè, almeno fino al 1861, dove sopraggiunsero i Savoia, che essendo dell'estremo Nord, non favorirono per nulla le regioni più remote del Regno. Spiace dirlo ma fu solo dai primi del Novecento che s'iniziò ad ammodernare il Sud, soprattutto col Fascismo, che iniziò con la costruzione degli apparati minimi statali; da qui la nostalgia di Mussolini che hanno molti anziani del Sud; per non parlare dei voti del 1946, che al Sud furono maggiormente orientati al mantenimento della Monarchia.
Il Nord, come già detto, ebbe storia diversa dal basso medioevo in poi: Comuni, Rinascimento, Signorie, Repubbliche Marinare e molta, moltissima, guerra, con lo zampino degli stati Europei. Quest'ultimi, Francia e Austria-Ungheria in primis, diedero un imprinting modernista ai piccoli Ducati e regni del Centro Nord (oltre a rubare tutto ciò che c'era da rubare), Lombardia in primis.
A mio modesto parere il Sud Italia viene da una situazione di arretratezza di lunghissimo corso dovuto principalmente al tipo di monarchia che hanno subito anche in tempi dove il resto d'Europa correva verso la modernità. Oggi la situazione è ben diversa, ma ci vorrà davvero ancora molto tempo per cambiare una cultura così ben radicata.
Per quanto riguarda lo sfavore ai disastri ambientali sono d'accordo fino ad un certo punto, altrimenti il Giappone dovrebbe essere lo stato più depresso al mondo, e non lo è.

Author: @maryrosarycota9522
Content:
The name of the island comes from the romanized god Vulcan, hence Vulcano in Italian. Vulcano  is the correspondent of the Greek god of fire Hēphaistos, latinized Hephaestus. The island of Vulcano in Sicily is the site attributed to Vulcan's furnace/forge. The switch from "u" to "o" in the English spelling may be due to the influence of the French language, as the word volcanic derives from the  French adjective volcanique (rather than the Latin noun, name of the god), which originally also has its roots in  the Latin form "Vulcanus" of the word. All of the romance languages share their origins in Latin. French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian and Spanish ( including Catalan) are  stems  so crossovers are inevitable.
 BTWY, someone wrote in this thread that 80% of English words come from Italian. Not so. A conspicuous amount of words come from Latin and have trickled down through romance languages as well. So Italian, as other romance languages, are spinoffs deriving from the original. 
On the other hand, the original Germanic/Frisian origins are the backbone of English, where  the majority of common, everyday words in our vocabulary can be found, so we can be thankful for all those irregular verbs still in use today😂. And the Scandinavian contributions are equally important too.  English is an extremely "bastardized" language, which actually gives it its strength and fortune today. Content: I'm a retired US Air Force officer, and my last duty station was Aviano Air Base, Italy, located about an hour north of Venice. In talking with the locals, I was told that the northern Italians refer to the southern Italians with the pejorative "terrani," and the southern Italians similarly refer to the northern Italians as "polani." The terms don't have exact English translations, but the closest American English equivalent for terrani would be "hillbillies," implying that the southern Italians are unsophisticated country bumpkins. The pejorative polani means something like "corn people," or "corn eaters." which is a reference to polenta, a corn meal dish that is a northern Italian dietary staple. The pejorative is similar to Mexicans being called "beaners" or "bean eaters."

Content:
All of my grandparents left southern Italy to work in major industries in the US. And those that had been sharecroppers were so eager to never touch the soil again that they completely urbanized themselves once they got here.

And I'm glad you mentioned the earthquakes.  My paternal grandpop and his family came from a little town in Potenza called Marsicovetere that was flattened by a deadly earthquake in 1857.  It was almost 150 years until their population rose back to what it had been before the quake because of the deaths and utterly massive emigration.

Author: @cavulocappoccio7690
Content:
While correctly underlining the historical importance of fairly recent feudalism in Southern Italy you failed to mention how that social form actually never stopped de facto existing even after the unification and became known as what we today call Mafia. Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian one, literally means 'our thing' or 'our business', as opposed to a centralized control. This condition of internal struggle has been essential in keeping the South underdeveloped, as any kind of development had, and in many ways still has, to pass through the Mafia and be directly controlled by it, according to its interests. In Palermo there has been basically a 20 years long civil war between the Mafia and the State, often with several daily deaths, for the control of the whole economy of Sicily, and similar conditions arose in Naples, historically they come and go in long waves. Nowadays the Mafia and the State have mostly decided to cooperate as long as everyone gets their share and the violence has greatly reduced, but local interests and local dominance, along with the lack of a solid enough historic basis to build upon, are still a huge limit to a more reasonable development effort.
It's also interesting to notice how many areas of Southern Italy had developed some impressive local economies around elite-level micro-industries during the '60s economic boom, just to be mostly engulfed and then abandoned by bigger Northern industries, castrating a really interesting and promising sprout of development.
On a side note, after all, as an Italian my self, I can say that the statist I can't now recall the name was right: Italy is, and should have been kept, a geographical definition. Independence should've come a completely different way.

Author: @Ricky911_
Content:
I've lived in 3 parts of Italy: rural Apulia (Southern Italy), Rome (central), Turin (Northern).  So, I wanna give my opinions on these issues. The difference between the 3 places is very noticeable. Here in Turin, life isn't so bad. It's not perfect by any means but I did prefer my life in the UK overall tbh (I've lived there for 4 years). In Rome, life was a bit worse. It's livable but, for example, it has a massive problem with garbage disposal, having streets filled with garbage, unlike Turin. However, my life in rural Apulia was horrific.

First of all, my small city looked exactly like this (6:50). It was just ugly buildings with streets drowned in cars and no trees. Other than the utter ugliness Southern cities have to offer, there are a whole set of cultural issues that need to be mentioned. I'll start off by saying that the map at 3:35 is very misleading. In Southern Italy, there is a big issue with people working illegally with no contract. While the official data shows low employment, a lot of people work illegally and pay no taxes. This, however, is also a problem for the workers since no taxing doesn't usually imply a high wage, as it's all illegal after all. Here in the North, working illegally is significantly less common. It's also one of the reasons there is turmoil between Northern Italians and Southern Italians. For example, Northern Italy generally votes right wing. A few years ago, the most popular party used to be Lega (originally Lega Nord), which mostly promoted policies to help the North. Southern Italians tend to vote for the Movement 5 Stars, which is a populist party.

Having said that, Rome is the capital so, it's worth noting that such a status automatically helps it be somewhat livable. However, it is a super corrupt city with terrible infrastructure and just management overall. In fact, Milan is the economic powerhouse of Italy despite it never having been the capital. 

Turin is actually pretty nice overall. Buildings are not ugly like in Apulia, there are quite a few trees, people don't usually park in weird places like in Rome and, as I said, things tend to work a lot better, There is no issue with garbage, the infrastructure is pretty developed and most laws are usually upheld. Overall, Turin is a nice city and the best place out of everywhere I've lived in Italy. 

Having said this, you mentioned it and I kind of hinted at it but the main two problems are culture and Geography. From a Geographical point of view, we are in a much better situation in the North, with the only drawback being the bad air quality caused by the Alps and the Apennines.  However, the cultural problem definitely needs a mention. Northern Italians are much more similar to Germans in the sense that they tend to be pretty strict with things. If a project needs to be finished within a certain time or there is a law to uphold, people will usually try to do their best to make sure these norms are followed. On the other hand, in Southern Italy, anything goes. To give an example, here in Turin, if you ride a moped without a helmet, you will probably be arrested as I have never even seen that happen here. On the other hand, anywhere in Southern Italy, you will regularly see riders with no helmet. Having said that, the South is also less educated and this can be seen in the fact that local dialects are still more spoken in Southern Italy than standard Italian. As you can see here (20:43), my current region already had a 51% literacy rate and it makes sense since Piedmont is the unifier of Italy, with Turin having been the first capital of Italy. In fact, not only do people here not have an accent, they also don't speak dialect at all. Piedmontese dialect is dead. Piedmont, Lombardy and Veneto were regions heavily influenced by France and Austria, which means they learned how to industrialise and how to administer a society. At the same time. Southern Italy was borderline feudal and it was super corrupt. These cultural aspects can still be felt. Northern Italians are stereotypically imagined as a bunch of workaholics, while Southern Italians are stereotyped as siesta enjoyers but, I can confirm these stereotypes are true. Southern Italy may have a Geographical disadvantage but, as someone who has spent 9 years of their childhood there, I can tell you the biggest problem is culture. If you asked a bunch of Northerners and a bunch of Sourtherners to set up a business, Northerners will always do it best. Quite frankly, I just can't stand the South and I only really go back to see my family.

Thank you for coming to my Ted Talk
